prompt: Put C4's abstractions in order from the largest to the smallest.
hint: Each one is made of the next.
trap: A component lives inside a container, never the other way round.

prompt: What does C4 prescribe, given that it does not prescribe shapes or colours?
hint: Lesson 1's reading test asked for the same things.

choices.text: The exact symbols for databases and queues
choices.why: A database may be a cylinder or a box; C4 leaves shapes to the author and asks for a legend.

choices.text: That diagrams be drawn in UML
choices.why: C4 borrows from UML at the code level, and is deliberately notation independent.

choices.text: What every box and line must say
choices.why: Right: a name, a type, a technology and a description on every element, and a labelled line for every relationship. The words are fixed; the drawing is free.

choices.text: A maximum of twelve elements per diagram
choices.why: There is no such limit in C4; twelve was lesson 1's rule of thumb for a question's scope.

prompt: This is Carcará's system context diagram with its words removed. Put each name on the part it belongs to.
hint: One box is solid and in the middle; the others on the right are dashed.

prompt: Frota belongs to Carcará, yet it is drawn grey on the ticketing context diagram. Why?
hint: What does the colour separate?

choices.text: Because it is old and will be replaced soon
choices.why: Age is not what the colour says; a legacy system in scope would be drawn in the scope colour.

choices.text: It is outside the system being described
choices.why: Yes: grey means outside the scope, not outside the company.

choices.text: Because another company maintains it
choices.why: The lesson says Carcará owns Frota; ownership is not what the grey shows.

choices.text: Because it has no users
choices.why: It has users, and the exercise in the section asks you to find them.

prompt: Which of these do not belong on a system context diagram? Choose all that apply.
hint: It is the picture anybody can read.

choices.text: The booking database
choices.why: Yes: a container, which is the next level.

choices.text: HTTPS/JSON on every line
choices.why: Yes: protocols mean nothing to most of its readers.

choices.text: The cloud provider's load balancer
choices.why: Yes: infrastructure belongs on a deployment diagram.

choices.text: The payment gateway
choices.why: It is a software system the ticketing system depends on, which is exactly what the context shows.

prompt: The ticketing API runs as ten Docker containers in production. How many C4 containers is it?
hint: A C4 container is a kind of thing that runs, not a running copy.

choices.text: Ten, one per Docker container
choices.why: The word clash is exactly the trap; the ten copies appear on a deployment diagram.

choices.text: One
choices.why: Right: ten replicas of the same application are one container, drawn once.

choices.text: Zero; a Docker container is infrastructure
choices.why: The application inside is a container; the Docker runtime is where it runs.

choices.text: Two: the image and the running process
choices.why: The image is a deployment artefact; C4's container is the application.

prompt: Which of these are C4 containers? Choose all that apply.
hint: Could it be deployed, started or stopped on its own?

choices.text: A serverless function that resizes photos
choices.why: Yes: it runs and is deployed on its own.

choices.text: The single-page app running in the passenger's browser
choices.why: Yes: it has to be running for the system to work, even though it runs on somebody else's device.

choices.text: A JSON library compiled into the API
choices.why: It never runs by itself; it is code inside a container.

choices.text: The Redis instance holding seat holds
choices.why: Yes: a data store is a container.

prompt: On Carcará's container diagram, why does a slow SMS provider not slow down a purchase?
hint: Look at the line from the API to the broker.

choices.text: The API does not wait: a worker sends the SMS later
choices.why: Right: the dashed line and the separate worker take the provider out of the purchase's path.

choices.text: The SMS provider is outside the boundary
choices.why: Being external says nothing about whether anybody waits for it.

choices.text: Redis caches the messages
choices.why: Redis holds seats, not messages.

choices.text: The mobile app sends the SMS directly to the passenger
choices.why: No line on the diagram says that, and it would expose the provider's credentials.

prompt: In C4, a container is anything that must be ___ for the system to work: an application or a data store.
hint: A runtime boundary.

prompt: The container diagram has one arrow from the ticketing API to the payment gateway. What does the component diagram show for it?
hint: A relationship at one level is explained by relationships below it.

choices.text: The same single arrow, from the API's boundary
choices.why: The component diagram opens the box; it shows which part inside makes the call.

choices.text: The adapter and the webhook handler
choices.why: Yes: the adapter calls the gateway and the gateway calls the handler back. Two relationships at level 3 explain the one at level 2.

choices.text: No arrow, because external systems are left out
choices.why: External elements appear wherever a component talks to them.

choices.text: The gateway's own components
choices.why: Carcará does not know them; the gateway stays one grey box.

prompt: When does the lesson say a component diagram is worth drawing by hand rather than generating?
hint: What can a hand-drawn diagram say that code cannot?

choices.text: By default, since generated diagrams are ugly
choices.why: Looks are not the argument; generated diagrams are never wrong about what exists.

choices.text: When the team has spare time
choices.why: The lesson's cases are about value, not time.

choices.text: For each container, so that the set is complete
choices.why: The lesson calls the component diagram optional and the first to go stale.

choices.text: To show an intended change, before and after
choices.why: Right: a drawing can say what was intended, which the code cannot.

prompt: Which is the best reason the lesson gives for drawing the booking aggregate at the code level?
hint: Who reads it besides engineers?

choices.text: Product people and engineers argue about it
choices.why: Yes: a domain model the business also reads earns a picture the code cannot give them.

choices.text: The IDE is unable to show class hierarchies
choices.why: It can, and that is one reason code-level diagrams are usually unnecessary.

choices.text: C4 requires the four levels for each component
choices.why: C4 calls level 4 optional.

choices.text: Class diagrams stay current longer than code
choices.why: They go stale the fastest of all levels.

prompt: A class in the code cannot be placed in any component on the component diagram. What does the lesson conclude?
hint: Two possibilities, both worth knowing.

choices.text: The class should be deleted
choices.why: It may be essential; the problem is that the architecture does not account for it.

choices.text: A missing component, or undecided code
choices.why: Right: either the diagram misses a component, or the code grew something nobody decided. The consistency rule finds one of the two.

choices.text: Code-level diagrams are unreliable
choices.why: The finding is about the relationship between levels, not about the reliability of a level.

choices.text: It belongs to the container directly, not to a component
choices.why: Containers are made of components; a stray class is the gap to explain.

prompt: Match each supplementary C4 diagram to what it shows.
hint: Estate, time, infrastructure.

pairs.right: every system the organisation runs, with no system in the middle
how container instances map onto infrastructure

prompt: When does the lesson prefer a dynamic diagram to a sequence diagram?
hint: What does the reader already know?

choices.text: When the order and the waits matter most
choices.why: That is when a sequence diagram is better, because time is a dimension of the page.

choices.text: When the scenario has more than ten steps
choices.why: Length is not the criterion the lesson gives.

choices.text: When the reader already knows the boxes
choices.why: Right: numbers on familiar boxes tell the story fastest.

choices.text: When the system has no external dependencies
choices.why: External elements appear on both kinds.

prompt: A container diagram shows a load balancer in front of the API. Where does the lesson say it belongs?
hint: Infrastructure, regions, replicas and counts.

choices.text: On the context diagram
choices.why: That one shows no technology or infrastructure at all.

choices.text: On the component diagram of the API
choices.why: A load balancer is not part of the API's code.

choices.text: On a deployment diagram
choices.why: Yes: it is where containers run, not a container.

choices.text: It stays; a load balancer is a container
choices.why: It is infrastructure; on a container diagram it mixes two kinds of picture.

prompt: Two APIs write to one database, and the diagram shows it accurately. What does the lesson say it hides?
hint: Who has to agree to a schema change?

choices.text: The database's technology
choices.why: The technology can be written on the cylinder; ownership cannot be inferred from it.

choices.text: That schema changes now need two teams to agree
choices.why: Yes: the missing owner is the most important fact about that database.

choices.text: The number of replicas
choices.why: That belongs on a deployment diagram and is not the point here.

choices.text: That the database is slow
choices.why: Nothing on the picture or in the lesson says so.

prompt: Match each case to where it belongs in C4.
hint: Could it run on its own?

pairs.left: a library shared by two services
pairs.right: a component or code in each

pairs.left: a module inside a modular monolith

prompt: Rui asks for one diagram to plan a database migration: which containers read and write the booking database, and over what. Which C4 diagram, and why?
hint: Which level shows data stores and protocols?

choices.text: The context diagram, because it is the simplest
choices.why: It shows no database at all.

choices.text: A component diagram for each container
choices.why: Far more detail than the question needs, and several diagrams instead of one.

choices.text: A deployment diagram, because databases are infrastructure
choices.why: A managed database's placement is deployment; who uses it, and how, is the container view.

choices.text: Level 2, limited to the store's readers and writers
choices.why: Right: containers and labelled lines with protocols, for one question.

prompt: A box on a container diagram reads only Ticketing. What could a reader take it to be?
hint: Lesson 1 found five meanings for Booking.

choices.text: A service, a team, a schema, or the whole system
choices.why: Yes: without a type and technology, the name could be any of them.

choices.text: The ticketing API, since it is a container diagram
choices.why: The diagram's level does not tell the reader what this box is; the type would.

choices.text: A person, since it has no technology
choices.why: People have a shape and a type of their own.

choices.text: Little; readers skip an unlabelled box
choices.why: Readers do not ignore it; they guess, and they guess differently.
